lesson.title: The Psychology of Work
lesson.summary: The branch of psychology that applies psychological science to the workplace, covering both the individual side of work, hiring, training, and performance, and the group and organizational side, motivation, leadership, and culture.
lesson.body:
Industrial-organizational psychology, usually shortened to I-O psychology, is the applied field that takes the tools and findings of psychological science and puts them to work in real organizations. It is traditionally described as having two overlapping halves. The industrial side focuses on the individual employee: how jobs should be analyzed and designed, how to fairly and validly select and train employees, and how to measure job performance well. The organizational side focuses on the group and the system: what motivates people at work, what makes leadership effective, what shapes job satisfaction and well being, and how an organization's structure and culture affects everyone in it. Both halves depend heavily on social norms, since a workplace is one of the settings where unwritten rules, about effort, hierarchy, communication, and fairness, shape behavior as much as any official policy.

Attribution theory turns out to matter enormously in this field, particularly in how managers evaluate performance. When a manager decides why an employee performed well or poorly, whether that outcome gets attributed to the employee's own ability and effort, a dispositional attribution, or to circumstances outside the employee's control, like a difficult client, faulty equipment, or an unrealistic deadline, a situational attribution, can change the manager's rating, feedback, and decisions about promotion or discipline substantially, sometimes more than the objective facts of the performance itself justify. Managers, like people generally, are vulnerable to the fundamental attribution error, the well documented tendency to overweight a person's disposition and underweight their situation when explaining someone else's behavior, which in a workplace can mean an employee gets blamed personally for a problem that was really caused by a bad process, poor training, or an unreasonable workload.

I-O psychology also draws heavily on the group phenomena covered elsewhere in this unit, since organizations are essentially collections of groups. Social loafing is a central concern in any organization that relies on team based work, and much of the field's research on performance measurement exists specifically to counter it by keeping individual contributions identifiable. Groupthink is a recognized risk in executive teams and boards that are cohesive, insulated, and under pressure to reach fast consensus. Social facilitation is relevant to how open workspaces, monitored call centers, and performance reviews conducted in front of peers can help or hurt an employee's output depending on how well practiced their tasks are.

The field has a long history, with early figures like Hugo Munsterberg in the early twentieth century among the first psychologists to apply psychological testing and methods directly to hiring and workplace efficiency questions. One of the most historically influential lines of research is the Hawthorne studies, a series of experiments conducted at the Western Electric Hawthorne Works starting in the 1920s, originally investigating how factors like lighting affected worker productivity. The often repeated finding, that workers' productivity increased simply because they knew they were being studied and attended to, became known as the Hawthorne effect and shaped decades of thinking about motivation and attention at work. Later statistical reanalyses of the original data have raised real questions about how cleanly that interpretation holds up, so the Hawthorne studies today are best treated as historically foundational and thought provoking rather than as a precisely established finding.
